title: Digital Wallet
prompt: Design a digital wallet where users hold a balance and send money to each other instantly. It must handle tens of thousands of transfers per second, and the books must always balance.

clarify.q: Is this stored value inside our system only, or do transfers also go to banks and cards?
clarify.why: Internal transfers are ledger moves we fully control. External ones involve slow partners that can fail hours later, which needs a different state machine and reconciliation against their files.

clarify.q: What peak transfer rate must we support?
clarify.why: A few hundred per second fits in one Postgres primary with plain transactions. Tens of thousands forces sharding, which is where all the hard parts of this problem begin.

clarify.q: Can a balance ever go negative?
clarify.why: If never, every debit needs a check against a strongly consistent balance at the moment of the transfer, which constrains how we shard and cache.

clarify.q: Must the receiver see the money instantly, or is a few seconds acceptable?
clarify.why: Instant for both sides across shards needs 2PC or a single ordering point. A few seconds lets the credit happen in a second step (a saga).

clarify.q: Are there very hot accounts, like a merchant receiving thousands of payments per second?
clarify.why: One balance row can only take a few hundred locked updates per second. Hot accounts need split balances or batching.

clarify.q: Which currencies, and do we convert between them?
clarify.why: Multi-currency means amounts in minor units per currency and FX as a separate pair of ledger entries, never mixing currencies in one balance.

clarify.q: What audit and retention rules apply?
clarify.why: Financial regulators usually want an immutable history for years. That pushes us to append-only entries and corrections as new entries, never updates.

functional: Users hold a balance per currency and can see it and their transaction history.
A user transfers money to another user. It either completes fully or not at all.
Top up from and withdraw to an external bank or card through a payment provider.
Every money movement is recorded as balanced double-entry ledger entries.
Retried requests never move money twice.
nonFunctional: Correctness first: total of all ledger entries is always zero; no money created or lost.
Sustain 30 k transfers/s at peak, p99 under 500 ms to a final status for internal transfers.
Sender's balance never goes below zero (no overdraft).
Ledger is immutable and retained for at least 7 years.
99.99% availability for reads of balances; transfers may reject under partial outage but never corrupt.
outOfScope: Fraud scoring models (we call a fraud service).
Card issuing and the card network side.

assumptions: 200 M transfers per day, peak 10× the average rate
Each internal transfer writes 2 ledger entries (debit and credit); fees would add more
One ledger entry ≈ 400 bytes including indexes
A Postgres shard sustains about 3 k transfer transactions/s with headroom
A locked balance row update takes about 2 ms end to end

steps.label: Shards needed
steps.result: 16 shards gives room to grow and a power of two

steps.label: Cross-shard share
steps.math: Random placement over 16 shards: chance both users share a shard = 1/16 ≈ 6%

steps.label: Hot account ceiling
steps.math: 1 row, 2 ms per locked update → 1 000 ms / 2 ms
steps.result: ≈ 500 updates/s max on one balance row

estimates.takeaway: The numbers say three things. One database will not do it, so we shard by account. Once sharded, almost every transfer crosses shards, so a single local transaction can no longer cover both sides; that is the core of the problem. And any account receiving more than about 500 payments/s needs a split balance. Storage growth (58 TB/year) is large but append-only, so older entries move to cheaper storage.

api.body: { fromWallet, toWallet, amount, currency, note? } + Idempotency-Key header
api.note: Same key returns the same transfer, never a second one. Most complete within 500 ms; client can poll or get a push.
available excludes held funds of in-flight transfers.
Statement view from a read model, cursor-paginated by entry id.
Credits the wallet only after the provider confirms by webhook.

entities.name: LedgerEntry
fields: groups the entries of one movement
entities.why: The source of truth. Never updated or deleted. Corrections are new reversing entries.

entities.name: Account
entities.store: Postgres, same shard as its entries
fields: system accounts are ledger accounts too
cached sum of entries, updated in the same local txn
entities.why: Keeping balance next to entries on one shard lets one local transaction write the entry and update the balance together.

entities.name: Transfer
entities.why: The saga's state machine. A recovery worker scans for transfers stuck in one state too long.

entities.name: Outbox
entities.store: Same shard as the write that produced it
entities.why: Writes the next-step event in the same local transaction as the ledger change, so no step is ever lost between DB and queue.

data.note: Amounts are integers in minor units (cents), never floats. The invariant per transfer is: sum of debits equals sum of credits. Each shard can check its own entries locally; the global check runs in reconciliation. Balances are a projection of entries kept in the same row-level transaction for fast checks; history and statements are separate read models (CQRS) fed by the outbox, so heavy statement queries never touch the write path.

hld.summary:
A transfer API validates the request, checks the idempotency key, calls fraud checks, and creates a Transfer record. A saga orchestrator then drives it: step one runs on the sender's shard and, in one local transaction, debits the sender and credits a transit account on that shard. Step two runs on the receiver's shard and debits that shard's transit account and credits the receiver. Each step writes its next event to an outbox, relayed to a queue, so the orchestrator advances even after crashes.

If both wallets are on the same shard, both steps run in one local transaction and the saga collapses to a single step. A projection pipeline consumes ledger events to build statements and analytics. Reconciliation jobs continuously check that all entries sum to zero, transit accounts net to the value of in-flight transfers, and our provider accounts match the banks' settlement files.

diagram.title: Cross-shard transfer with a saga
diagram.src:
flowchart LR
  C[Client] --> API[Transfer API]
  API --> FR[Fraud service]
  API --> TR[(Transfers DB)]
  API --> ORC[Saga orchestrator]
  ORC --> SA[(Ledger shard A sender)]
  ORC --> SB[(Ledger shard B receiver)]
  SA --> OB[Outbox relay]
  SB --> OB
  OB --> Q[Event queue]
  Q --> ORC
  Q --> PRJ[Statement projections]
  Q --> REC[Reconciliation]

flows.title: Alice sends 50.00 to Bob on another shard
steps: API stores Transfer T1 (CREATED) keyed by Alice's idempotency key, then hands it to the orchestrator.
Shard A, one local txn: check Alice's balance ≥ 5 000 cents, debit Alice 5 000, credit transit-A 5 000, write outbox event Debited. T1 → DEBITED.
Shard B, one local txn: debit transit-B 5 000, credit Bob 5 000, write Credited. Unique (transferId, step) makes a retried step a no-op. T1 → CREDITED.
Orchestrator marks T1 COMPLETED and notifies both users. Transit-A is +5 000 and transit-B is −5 000; across shards they net to zero.

flows.title: Bob's wallet is frozen
steps: Step two fails with a permanent error: receiver frozen.
Orchestrator moves T1 to COMPENSATING and runs the reverse on shard A: debit transit-A 5 000, credit Alice 5 000.
T1 → FAILED. Alice's balance is restored; the history shows the debit and its reversal, never a deleted row.

flows.title: Top-up from a bank card
steps: API creates a pending top-up and calls the payment provider with our idempotency key.
Provider webhook confirms. One local txn: debit provider-clearing account, credit the user's wallet.
Daily settlement file from the provider is matched against provider-clearing entries; mismatches go to a breaks queue.

deepDives.title: Double-entry ledger model
deepDives.problem: A naive wallet has a balance column and does UPDATE balance = balance - 50. A bug, a retry, or a partial failure then silently creates or destroys money, and there is no record to explain why a balance is what it is.

options.name: Mutable balance column only
options.how: Update balances in place; keep a loose transaction log for display.
pros: Simple, fast reads
cons: No invariant to check
Audit relies on a log that can drift from balances
Corrections overwrite history

options.name: Double-entry, append-only entries with cached balances
options.how: Every movement writes at least one debit and one credit whose amounts sum to zero. Balance = sum of an account's entries; cached on the account row and updated in the same local txn.
pros: Invariant is checkable at any time: total of all entries is zero
Every balance can be explained entry by entry
System accounts (fees, transit, provider clearing) make every movement visible
cons: At least twice the rows of a single-entry log
Developers must think in accounts, including internal ones

deepDives.choice: Double-entry, append-only. The extra rows are the price of a provable invariant, and storage (≈ 58 TB/year) is manageable with tiering. The cached balance is protected by a DB check constraint (balance >= 0 for user accounts) and updated in the same transaction as its entries, so it can never disagree with them on one shard. I would only drop the cache and derive balances on read for low-volume accounts where reads are rare.

deepDives.title: Why one database transaction stops working
deepDives.problem: With one database, a transfer is easy: BEGIN; debit Alice; credit Bob; COMMIT. At 30 k transfers/s we need about 10–16 shards, and 94% of transfers then have Alice and Bob on different machines. No single local transaction can cover both rows. Separately, a merchant receiving 2 k payments/s hits the 500 updates/s limit of a single locked row.

options.name: Shard so related accounts colocate
options.how: Place accounts that often transact together on the same shard (family, a merchant and its frequent buyers).
pros: Some transfers stay local
cons: P2P graphs are not cleanly partitionable; most pairs still cross shards
Rebalancing breaks the colocation

options.name: Single global ledger with heavy batching
options.how: Keep one ordering point for all transfers, but process them in large batches per commit (thousands per fsync), on a purpose-built ledger store.
pros: Every transfer is atomic, no sagas
Batching gives very high throughput on one node
cons: Specialized technology or a lot of custom engineering
One ordering point limits geographic distribution

options.name: Shard by account and coordinate across shards
options.how: Each shard owns its accounts and balances. A cross-shard transfer becomes a multi-step protocol (2PC or saga).
pros: Standard databases, scales by adding shards
cons: Needs a coordination protocol and in-between states

deepDives.choice: Shard by account and coordinate, since it uses standard databases and grows linearly. For hot accounts, split the balance: a merchant account becomes N sub-accounts on the same shard (say 8), credits go to a random sub-account, and the total is their sum. That raises the ceiling from about 500 to about 4 000 credits/s. Debits from a split account (merchant payouts) are rare and can lock all sub-accounts. If the team had a proven high-throughput ledger store available, the single global ledger would be simpler to get right, and I would seriously consider it.

deepDives.title: Sagas vs two-phase commit
deepDives.problem: Cross-shard transfers need all-or-nothing behavior. Two-phase commit gives atomicity but holds locks across a network round trip. A saga avoids distributed locks but exposes an in-between state where money has left Alice and not yet reached Bob.

options.name: Two-phase commit across shards
options.how: Coordinator asks both shards to prepare (lock rows, write prepare record), then commits on both.
pros: Atomic: both sides visible at once
No compensation logic
cons: Locks held for two round trips plus fsyncs (about 5–10 ms instead of 1–2 ms), cutting hot-row throughput several times
If the coordinator dies after prepare, rows stay locked until it recovers
Not all managed databases expose prepared transactions safely

options.name: Orchestrated saga with transit accounts
options.how: Step 1 on shard A: debit sender, credit transit-A. Step 2 on shard B: debit transit-B, credit receiver. Failure after step 1 runs a compensation that reverses it. Each step is idempotent on (transferId, step).
pros: Only local transactions, locks held about 2 ms
Each shard independently consistent; transit accounts make in-flight money visible on the books
Easy to resume after crashes from the Transfer state
cons: Receiver sees money a few hundred ms after the sender loses it
Compensation must be designed for every step
More states to monitor (stuck sagas)

options.name: Choreographed saga (events, no orchestrator)
options.how: Shard A emits Debited; shard B listens and credits; failures emit events that A listens to.
pros: No central component
cons: The flow is spread across services and hard to trace or change
Stuck transfers are harder to find

deepDives.choice: Orchestrated saga with transit accounts. Debit first, credit second: if anything stops in the middle, money is held in a transit account, never created. The in-between state is acceptable because the product promise is 'Bob gets it within a second'. The orchestrator is stateless; state lives in the Transfer row, and outbox events push each step. A sweeper retries transfers stuck more than 30 s and alerts after 5 minutes. I would choose 2PC if the business required that no one could ever observe the in-between state, and the volume per account were low enough to absorb the longer locks.

diagram.title: Saga steps and compensation
diagram.src:
sequenceDiagram
  participant O as Orchestrator
  participant A as Shard A
  participant B as Shard B
  O->>A: step 1 T1, debit Alice, credit transit-A
  A-->>O: Debited via outbox
  O->>B: step 2 T1, debit transit-B, credit Bob
  alt credit succeeds
    B-->>O: Credited
    O->>O: T1 COMPLETED
  else receiver frozen
    B-->>O: permanent failure
    O->>A: compensate T1, debit transit-A, credit Alice
    A-->>O: Reversed
    O->>O: T1 FAILED
  end

deepDives.title: Event sourcing and CQRS for audit
deepDives.problem: Auditors ask: what was this user's balance on 3 March at 14:00, and why? Support asks for a statement of the last 90 days. Analysts want daily volumes. None of these should slow down the transfer path.

options.name: Ledger entries as the event log, projections for reads
options.how: Ledger entries plus transfer state changes are the immutable event stream. Projections consume them (via outbox and queue) into statement tables, search, and a warehouse.
pros: Balance at any time = sum of entries up to that time
Read models can be rebuilt from scratch
Write path stays small
cons: Read models lag by seconds
Rebuilding a projection over years of data takes hours

options.name: Query the ledger shards directly
options.how: Statements and reports query the sharded write database.
pros: Always current
cons: Heavy scans compete with transfers
Cross-shard reports are painful

deepDives.choice: Ledger as event log plus CQRS projections. The ledger already is an event store: append-only, ordered per account, never edited. Balance checks for transfers use the cached balance on the shard (strong); statements use the projection (seconds behind, and labeled with asOfEntryId). For fast point-in-time answers, store a daily closing balance per account. If regulators required a tamper-evident log, I'd add a hash chain over each shard's entries and publish daily roots.

deepDives.title: Reconciliation
deepDives.problem: Bugs, half-finished sagas, duplicate webhooks and partner errors will happen. We need to find any break within hours, before customers or auditors do.

options.name: Internal invariant checks
options.how: Continuous jobs check: entries per transfer sum to zero; cached balances equal sums of entries; sum of all transit accounts equals the amount of transfers in DEBITED state.
pros: Catches our own bugs quickly
Cheap when run incrementally by entry id
cons: Cannot see errors at external partners

options.name: External reconciliation against partner files
options.how: Daily, match provider and bank settlement files line by line to our provider-clearing entries by reference id and amount.
pros: Catches missing or duplicated external money movements
cons: Partners report late and in odd formats
Matching rules (fees, FX rounding) are fiddly

deepDives.choice: Run both. Internal checks run every few minutes on new entries and fully each night per shard. External matching runs when each settlement file lands. Every mismatch becomes a 'break' with an owner and an age; fixes are new correcting entries with a reason code, never edits. A good target is: zero unexplained internal breaks, and external breaks resolved within 2 business days. If break volume grew, I'd add auto-resolution rules for known patterns (for example a webhook delayed past cutoff).

failures: Transfer row says DEBITED. Another instance picks it up from the sweeper or the outbox event and runs step 2. Steps are idempotent on (transferId, step).
Client retries a POST after a timeout
Idempotency key is unique per sender. The second request returns the original transfer and its current status.
Step 2 retries with backoff; money waits in transit-A and the sender sees 'pending'. After a timeout (for example 10 minutes) compensate and mark FAILED.
Provider sends the same webhook twice
Unique constraint on (provider, providerEventId) before crediting. The second one is a no-op.
A bug writes an unbalanced entry
A DB-level trigger or commit-time check per transfer rejects it on the shard; reconciliation alerts if anything slips through.
Hot merchant account causes lock waits
Split into sub-accounts; queue and batch credits if it still saturates.
scale: 10× transfers: go from 16 to 64+ shards. Use logical shards (for example 1 024) mapped to physical hosts so moving load does not require re-hashing accounts.
Hot accounts: increase sub-accounts, or batch credits every 100 ms into one entry per merchant with line items in a side table.
Storage: partition entries by month; move entries older than 13 months to cheap columnar storage, keeping daily closing balances hot.
Multi-region: home each wallet in one region; cross-region transfers are sagas across regions with longer timeouts.

followups.q: How do you prevent double spending when two transfers from the same wallet race?
answer: Step 1 runs as a local transaction that locks the sender's row (SELECT … FOR UPDATE or a conditional UPDATE balance = balance − x WHERE balance ≥ x).
Only one debit commits at a time per account; the second sees the new balance.
Because the debit happens on the sender's shard first, no cross-shard check is needed for overdraft.

followups.q: How would you handle currency conversion?
answer: Each currency has its own accounts; a balance never mixes currencies.
A conversion debits the user in USD and credits an FX account in USD, then debits the FX account in EUR and credits the user in EUR, at a quoted rate.
Rate quotes are stored with the transfer for audit; FX accounts are reconciled with the liquidity provider.
A refund is a new transfer in the opposite direction linked to the original.
Never edit or delete the original entries.
Partial refunds are just smaller amounts; checks prevent refunding more than the original.

followups.q: How do you show an accurate balance while a transfer is in flight?
answer: Show available (after debits) and pending incoming separately.
The sender's available drops at step 1, so they cannot spend the money twice.
The receiver sees it as available only after step 2 commits.

followups.q: Why not use Kafka as the ledger?
answer: Kafka gives ordering per partition but no conditional writes, so it cannot enforce 'no overdraft' by itself.
You would rebuild balance checks in a consumer, which is a database anyway.
Kafka is a good transport for outbox events and projections, not the source of truth here.

mistakes: Updating a balance column with no entries behind it.
Assuming one database transaction still works after sharding.
Crediting the receiver before debiting the sender in a saga, which creates money on failure.
Forgetting idempotency on every step, not just the API.

mid: Used integer minor units for amounts
Recorded each transfer as a debit and a credit that sum to zero
Added an idempotency key on the transfer API
Prevented overdraft with a locked or conditional update
senior: Computed shard count and the cross-shard fraction from the numbers
Explained why a single local transaction fails after sharding
Designed a saga with debit first, credit second, and a compensation path
Used an outbox so steps are not lost between DB and queue
Separated read models (statements) from the write path
staff: Compared 2PC and sagas on lock duration, failure modes and user-visible states, and named when 2PC wins
Handled hot accounts with split balances and gave the new ceiling
Designed internal and external reconciliation with breaks, owners and correcting entries
Used transit or clearing accounts so in-flight money is visible on the books
